lessons.title: Family Types and Structures
lessons.content:
The family is the basic unit of society. In the Caribbean, family structures are diverse and influenced by our rich history and cultural heritage. The 'Nuclear Family' consists of a mother, father, and their children living together. The 'Extended Family' includes other relatives like grandparents, aunts, or cousins living in the same household or nearby.

Other common structures include the 'Single-parent Family' (one parent raising children), the 'Reconstituted' or 'Blended Family' (formed when parents with children from previous relationships marry), and 'Common-law Relationships' (where a couple lives together without being legally married). Sib-link households, where brothers and sisters live together without parents, are also found in some communities.

CSEC Social Studies students must be able to identify these types and discuss their characteristics. Understanding family diversity is essential for appreciating the different ways Caribbean people live and support one another. The family's role in providing emotional and economic stability is a key topic of discussion.

The terms that go with these types matter as much as the types themselves. A Household is the group of people who share one dwelling and one cooking pot; a family is a group related by blood, marriage or adoption, so a household may hold more than one family and a family may live in more than one household. A Conjugal Family is built on the union of two adults and their children; a Consanguineous Family is built on blood ties, so a grandmother raising her daughter's children heads a consanguineous household. A Matrifocal Household is one in which the mother, or the grandmother, is the centre of authority and the household's stability, a pattern found across the Caribbean and explained by migration, wage work and the history of the plantation.

Families are formed through unions, and the Caribbean recognises three. Marriage is the legal union registered with the state and often blessed by a church. A common-law union is a stable partnership without a marriage certificate, and it is common in the region. A Visiting Union is a relationship in which partners live at different addresses and one visits the other, often because of work, school or housing, and the children of the union usually live with the mother. Naming the union correctly matters in an exam answer, because each carries different legal rights to maintenance, inheritance and custody.
objectives: Identify different types of families in the Caribbean
Describe the characteristics of each family type
Define the family and the household, and the terms used to describe them
Describe the unions through which Caribbean families are formed

experiment.description: Family Tree Builder: Drag and drop family members to create different family structures and see how they are defined.

lessons.title: Roles and Responsibilities
lessons.content:
Within every family, members have specific roles and responsibilities that contribute to the household's functioning. Traditionally, roles were often divided by gender (division of labour), but in modern Caribbean society, these roles are increasingly shared. Parents have the primary responsibility for the 'socialisation' of their children — teaching them the values, norms, and skills needed to participate in society.

Responsible parenthood involve providing not just economic support (food, shelter, education) but also emotional support (love, guidance, protection). Children also have responsibilities, such as performing household chores and showing respect to their elders. As family members age, the roles may shift, with adult children taking on the care of their elderly parents.

Understanding these dynamics is crucial for discussing issues like family conflict, child abuse, and the impact of migration on family life. CSEC questions often ask you to analyse how changing social and economic conditions affect family roles and the importance of strong, supportive family units for a healthy society.

The family is not only a set of roles; it performs functions that no other institution performs in the same way. Reproduction is the function that replaces the population. Protection covers the young, the sick and the old, and it is the function the state most often has to support. Socialisation teaches the child the language, values and habits of the society, and it is the family's first and strongest contribution to social order. The economic function provides food, shelter and income, and it includes the unpaid work of cooking, cleaning and caring. Regulation of Sexual Behaviour sets the society's rules about who may pair with whom and in what form. Social Placement gives a child a religion, a class position and a place in the community.

Those roles are changing. Women's employment outside the home has made shared housework and shared childcare more common, and a Female-headed Household - one where the mother is the main earner and decision-maker - is now a large share of Caribbean households. Migration and Family Roles are linked: when a parent works abroad, the remaining parent takes on both roles, and the eldest child often becomes a young carer. Longer lives mean adult children may become the carers of their parents, reversing the role they were raised in. The change is not evenly spread: a household with one low income and no help carries the same roles with fewer resources, which is why the strain shows first in the poorest homes.
objectives: Examine the roles of family members
Understand the importance of responsible parenthood
State the functions the family performs for its members and for society
Explain how family roles are changing in the Caribbean

experiment.description: Role Assigner: Match various family tasks and responsibilities to different family members in a virtual household scenario.

lessons.title: Preparation for Parenthood
lessons.content:
Preparation for Parenthood is the work a couple or a household does before a child arrives, so that the child is wanted, provided for and safe. Readiness for Parenthood has four sides - emotional, financial, social and health - and a family that prepares on one side only is still unprepared on the others.

Emotionally, both partners should want the child and understand that a baby changes sleep, money and free time, so the decision belongs to the couple and not to one of them alone. Financially, the household needs a budget that covers food, clothing, housing, school and medical care, and a plan for who earns while a parent stays at home. Socially, the household needs a support network of grandparents, godparents, church and community groups that can help in an emergency, and a home that is safe for a crawling child.

Health preparation begins with Family Planning: advice from a health centre or doctor about whether and when to have a child, and about spacing children. Once a pregnancy is confirmed, Ante-natal Care means early booking at a clinic, regular checks with a midwife or doctor, a balanced diet with iron and folic acid, treatment for conditions such as high blood pressure or anaemia, and knowing the danger signs that mean going to hospital at once. Post-natal Care continues after the birth: checks for mother and baby, breastfeeding support, immunisations, and watching for depression in the mother.

Teenage pregnancy shows why preparation matters. A young mother who leaves school early often loses the qualifications the household will need, so counselling, continuing education and family support are part of the picture. Support Services in Jamaica include the public health system's antenatal and postnatal clinics, health centres, and church and community programmes that give parents advice and practical help.

The exam point: preparation is a process with stages - deciding, planning, ante-natal care, post-natal care - and every stage carries a named responsibility for the parents.
objectives: Explain what Preparation for Parenthood involves
Describe Ante-natal Care and Post-natal Care
Identify the emotional, financial and social support a household needs before a child arrives

experiment.description: Preparing for a Baby: match each preparation step to what it secures.

lessons.title: Effective Parenting
lessons.content:
Effective Parenting is the set of practices that help a child grow up healthy, confident and able to learn. It starts from the parenting styles sociologists describe. Authoritative Parenting sets firm, explained limits and listens to the child; young people raised this way tend to be confident and to do well at school. Authoritarian Parenting demands obedience without explanation and can leave a child obedient but anxious. Permissive Parenting sets few limits and few demands, which can leave a child without self-control.

The practices matter as much as the style. Consistency means the same rule is applied on Monday and on Saturday, and by both parents, so the child knows what to expect. Praise for effort teaches a child that trying is worthwhile, while praise only for results teaches fear of failing. Time spent talking and listening - about school, friends and worries - is what keeps a parent the person a child comes to first.

Positive Discipline is the approach the school curriculum recommends: explain the rule, warn before punishing, use natural consequences, and separate the child from the behaviour so the child is corrected without being humiliated. Jamaican law protects children from abuse, and school rules forbid beating in school, so a parent or teacher who can correct a child without hitting is doing what the law and the curriculum both expect.

Effective parenting also means knowing when to ask for help: from the school's guidance counsellor, the health centre, the Child Protection and Family Services Agency if a child is in danger, or a parenting programme. Both parents and guardians share the work, and a father's steady involvement is one of the strongest supports a child can have.
objectives: Distinguish the main parenting styles
Explain the practices that support a child's development
Describe Positive Discipline and why it works

experiment.description: Parenting Styles: match each style to the way it sets limits.

lessons.title: Social Issues Affecting Families
lessons.content:
Social Issues Affecting Families are the problems that damage a household from inside or outside it. CSEC asks you to name each issue, explain how it affects the family's members, and say what the family and the state can do about it.

Domestic Violence is abuse between people who live together or are related - physical, sexual, emotional or financial. Its effects reach the children who witness it, who may become anxious, withdrawn or violent themselves, and it often drives a parent and children out of the home. Substance Abuse - alcohol and drug misuse by a parent - takes money from food and school, and leaves children caring for younger siblings and for the parent.

Teenage Pregnancy interrupts a girl's education, ties her to an older partner, and often keeps a whole generation in poverty; the family absorbs the cost through the grandparents who end up raising the child. Migration and Absent Parents describe the household left behind when one or both parents work abroad: money arrives, but so do new responsibilities for the eldest child and long separations that weaken the parents' authority. Poverty underlies several of the others - crowded housing, poor nutrition, early school leaving - and it is the issue the state attacks most directly.

Responses come from three directions. The family responds with kinship care, where a grandmother, aunt or godparent takes in a child. The community responds through church, school and youth programmes, and through neighbours who report a child in danger. The state responds through the police, the courts and the Child Protection and Family Services Agency, through school feeding and the PATH programme, and through counselling and health services. Naming the response matters in an exam answer: a problem stated without a remedy earns half the marks.
objectives: Identify the social issues that affect Caribbean families
Explain how each issue affects the family's members
Describe the responses of the family, the community and the state

experiment.description: Name That Issue: match each situation to the social issue and its effect.

lessons.title: Laws Protecting the Family
lessons.content:
Laws Protecting the Family are the statutes and courts that stand behind a family member who is harmed, abandoned or denied support. In Jamaica the frameworks you should be able to name are these.

The Domestic Violence Act lets a person who is being abused apply to the court for a protection order against someone they live with or are related to, and the police may act on it. The Child Care and Protection Act makes it an offence to ill-treat, neglect or abandon a child, sets out who may care for a child, and gives the state the power to remove a child who is in danger. The Maintenance Act lets a parent or guardian apply to the court for maintenance - money for a child's food, clothing, school and medical care - from a parent who will not provide it. The Status of Children Act gives a child born outside marriage the same rights as a child born inside it, including the right to inherit and to be maintained by the father.

The Family Court is where most of this work is heard: maintenance, custody, access and protection orders. Where a family member can go for help matters as much as the law's name: the police for immediate danger, the Family Court for orders and maintenance, the Child Protection and Family Services Agency where a child is being harmed, a health centre or hospital for medical care and evidence, and the legal aid service for a lawyer when the applicant cannot pay for one.

Two exam habits pay here. First, state the protection the law gives, not just the Act's name - an answer that names the Domestic Violence Act and says a protection order can be applied for earns both marks. Second, remember that a statute is amended over time: quote the Act by name, describe what it protects, and check the current version with the Ministry of Justice or a lawyer before relying on a particular section or penalty.
objectives: Name the laws that protect family members in Jamaica
Explain what each law protects
Describe where a family member can go for help

experiment.description: Which Law Protects? Match each situation to the law and the help it gives.

lessons.title: Primary and Secondary Groups
lessons.content:
Humans are social beings who belong to many different groups. A 'Primary Group' is a small social group whose members share close, personal, and enduring relationships (like a family or a close circle of friends). These groups are characterised by face-to-face interaction and strong emotional ties. They play a vital role in our personal development and sense of identity.

A 'Secondary Group' is typically larger and more impersonal. These groups are often goal-oriented and formed for a specific purpose (like a professional organisation, a school club, or a large business). Interaction in secondary groups is more formal and less frequent than in primary groups. You may belong to a secondary group for years without forming deep personal connections with all its members.

CSEC students must be able to distinguish between these two types of groups and understand the characteristics that define them, such as group size, cohesion, and leadership styles. Recognising the different groups we belong to helps us understand how our behaviour and values are shaped by our social environment.

The concepts sociologists use to describe groups go beyond primary and secondary. An In-group is the group a person belongs to and feels loyalty toward; an Out-group is a group the person does not belong to, and the pair explains cliques, school rivalries and prejudice against newcomers. A Formal Group is organised with written rules, officers and stated purposes - a trade union, a school's students' council, a credit union. An Informal Group is a friendship or liming group with no officers and no written rules, held together by liking and habit. Group Norms are the unwritten rules a group enforces: what members wear, how they speak, what they must not say, and what happens to a member who breaks the rule, which is Conformity under pressure.

Group Cohesion is the strength of the bonds that hold members together, and it rises with shared goals, frequent face-to-face interaction, a size small enough for everyone to know everyone, and leadership that members trust. Cohesion is what makes a group able to act, and it is also what makes exclusion from it painful. Cohesion breaks when members stop meeting, when a dispute about leadership splits the group, when the shared goal is achieved or lost, or when the cost of belonging - subscriptions, time, loyalty tests - comes to outweigh what the member gets back. A group that has lost cohesion still exists on paper but no longer acts, which is why a youth club with empty meetings is an example of low cohesion rather than the end of the group.
objectives: Distinguish between primary and secondary groups
Understand the characteristics of groups
Explain the concepts used to describe social groups
Describe what holds a group together and what breaks it

experiment.description: Group Sorter: Categorise different social gatherings (e.g., a family dinner vs. a business meeting) into primary or secondary groups.

lessons.title: Social Institutions
lessons.content:
Social institutions are organised systems of social relationships that perform essential functions for society. The major institutions found in almost every culture include the Family, Religion, Education, the Economy, and the Justice System. Each institution has its own set of norms, values, and roles.

For example, the institution of Education is responsible for transmitting knowledge and skills, while Religion provides spiritual guidance and a sense of meaning. The Economy manages the production and distribution of goods and services, and the Justice System maintains order and protects the rights of citizens. These institutions are interconnected — changes in one often lead to changes in others.

In CSEC Social Studies, you will explore how these institutions function in the Caribbean and how they contribute to social stability or change. You will also discuss challenges facing these institutions, such as the impact of technology on education or the role of religion in modern secular societies.

Besides having functions, institutions share characteristics that let you recognise one. An Institutional Structure is the arrangement of positions and roles - the ministry, the school board, the head teacher, the class teacher - so that the work continues whoever holds the post. Persistence is the institution's survival beyond the people in it: a school outlives its head teachers and a church outlives its ministers. Group Norms become written rules in an institution, and Sanctions are the rewards and penalties that enforce them - a certificate, a promotion, a fine, exclusion. Legitimacy is the acceptance by the society that the institution has the right to do what it does, which is why a court's ruling is obeyed and a mob's is not. Interdependence is the fact that no institution stands alone: the school depends on the family to send the child, on the economy for tax revenue and on the justice system to enforce attendance, so a failure in one is felt in the others.
objectives: Identify major social institutions
Understand their functions in society
Describe the characteristics that social institutions share

experiment.description: Institution Matcher: Link social needs (e.g., 'spiritual guidance', 'learning skills') to the corresponding social institution.

lessons.title: Social Group Interaction
lessons.content:
Social Group Interaction is what happens when groups meet, work together or compete for the same things. Sociologists describe four forms. Cooperation is working together for a goal neither could reach alone, as a village does to build a road or a class does to stage a concert. Competition is striving for a scarce goal by rules - two schools for the same trophy, two firms for the same customers. Conflict is competition that has broken its rules and turned to harming the other side, whether between gangs, political parties or neighbours. Accommodation is the settlement that follows: a truce, a compromise, mediation, or an agreement to differ, and it is what makes cooperation possible again.

Groups sort people into In-group and Out-group. The in-group is the group a person belongs to and feels loyalty toward; the out-group is everyone else, and the danger is that loyalty to the in-group becomes hostility to the out-group - the mechanism behind cliques in school, rivalry between communities and discrimination against newcomers.

Peer Pressure is the influence a group has on its members to conform, and it works both ways: a group can press a young person toward study, sport and discipline, or toward truancy, violence and drug use. The group that rewards conformity most strongly is the one that matters most to the member, which is why the family and the school work to be that group.

Conflict between groups is not always bad - it can expose injustice and force change - but it is expensive, so societies build ways to accommodate it: bargaining through trade unions, mediation, elections that settle disputes without violence, and the courts. The exam point is to name the form of interaction first, then say what produced it and what settled it.
objectives: Describe the forms of interaction between social groups
Explain in-groups, out-groups and peer pressure
Discuss how conflict between groups can be resolved

experiment.description: Sort the Interaction: put each example under Cooperation, Competition, Conflict or Accommodation.

lessons.title: Systems of Government
lessons.content:
Government is the system by which a society is organised and controlled. In the Caribbean, we have several different systems. Many English-speaking countries are 'Constitutional Monarchies,' where the British Monarch is the ceremonial head of state, represented by a Governor-General. Others, like Trinidad and Tobago or Guyana, are 'Republics' with their own President as head of state.

A 'Democracy' is a system where power is held by the people, usually through elected representatives. Elections are held periodically, where citizens in different 'constituencies' vote for candidates. The party with the most seats in parliament typically forms the government. This contrasts with a 'Dictatorship,' where power is held by a single person or a small group with little or no input from the public.

Understanding these systems is vital for active citizenship. CSEC students learn about the electoral process, the role of political parties, and the importance of transparency and accountability in government. Knowing how your country is governed empowers you to participate in the democratic process and advocate for change.
objectives: Compare different systems of government in the Caribbean
Understand the democratic process

experiment.description: Election Day Simulation: Act as a voter or a candidate, understanding the process of casting ballots and how constituencies work.

lessons.title: The Branches of Government
lessons.content:
Most democratic governments are divided into three branches to ensure a 'separation of powers' and a system of 'checks and balances.' This prevents any one person or group from having too much control. The three branches are the Legislative, the Executive, and the Judiciary.

The 'Legislative' branch (the Parliament or National Assembly) is responsible for making and passing laws. The 'Executive' branch (the Prime Minister or President and their Cabinet) is responsible for implementing and enforcing those laws and managing the daily affairs of the country. The 'Judiciary' (the courts and judges) is responsible for interpreting the laws and ensuring they are applied fairly.

CSEC students must be able to identify the functions of each branch and explain how they work together. For example, the legislature may pass a law, but the judiciary can rule it unconstitutional if it violates the rights of citizens. Understanding this structure is essential for understanding how the justice system and the political system interact.
objectives: Identify the three branches of government
Explain the principle of separation of powers

experiment.description: Laws and Gavel: Trace a law from its proposal in parliament to its enforcement and interpretation by the courts.

lessons.title: CARICOM and Its Objectives
lessons.content:
Regional integration is the process where neighbouring countries cooperate to achieve common goals. In our region, the primary organisation is CARICOM (the Caribbean Community). Its main objectives include 'Economic Integration' (creating a single market and economy), 'Functional Cooperation' (sharing resources in areas like health, education, and disaster management), and 'Coordination of Foreign Policy.'

CARICOM member states work together to improve the lives of Caribbean people by creating more jobs, increasing trade, and providing a stronger voice in international affairs. Key initiatives include the CSME (CARICOM Single Market and Economy), which allows for the free movement of goods, services, and skilled labour across the region.

CSEC Social Studies students must know the member states of CARICOM and be able to discuss its purpose and achievements. You will also learn about other regional organisations like the OECS (Organisation of Eastern Caribbean States) and the importance of regional unity in a globalised world.
objectives: Explain the purpose of CARICOM
Identify the member states

experiment.description: Caribbean Map Quiz: Drag and drop Caribbean country flags to their correct locations and identify which are CARICOM members.

lessons.title: Benefits and Challenges
lessons.content:
Regional integration offers many benefits to Caribbean countries, but it also faces significant challenges. Benefits include 'Freedom of Movement' for people and goods, which can lead to increased trade and economic growth. Integration also allows for 'Standardisation' of products and services and better 'Regional Security' through cooperation between police and military forces.

However, challenges include differences in economic development between member states, which can lead to concerns about some countries benefiting more than others. Trade barriers, transport issues between islands, and the high cost of maintaining regional organisations are also obstacles. Some citizens may also fear that integration will lead to a loss of national identity.

CSEC questions often ask you to analyse these benefits and challenges and suggest ways to overcome them. Discussing regional integration helps you understand the importance of cooperation and the complex factors that influence the success of international organisations.
objectives: Discuss the benefits of regional integration
Identify challenges to integration

experiment.description: Trade Route Game: Move goods between Caribbean islands and see how removing trade barriers affects the speed and cost.

lessons.title: Population Distribution and Growth
lessons.content:
Population distribution refers to how people are spread across a specific area. Factors influencing this include climate, availability of resources (like water and fertile land), and economic opportunities (like jobs in cities). Caribbean populations are often concentrated along the coasts and in urban centres.

Population growth is determined by three main factors: birth rate, death rate, and migration. The 'Natural Increase' is the difference between the birth rate and the death rate. If the birth rate is higher, the population grows. A 'Population Pyramid' is a visual tool used to show the age and sex structure of a population, which helps governments plan for future needs in education, healthcare, and housing.

CSEC students will learn to calculate birth, death, and fertility rates and to interpret population pyramids. Understanding population dynamics is essential for discussing issues like urbanisation, the challenges of an ageing population, and the impact of population growth on the environment and resources.
objectives: Understand factors affecting population distribution
Calculate birth and death rates

experiment.description: Population Pyramid Builder: Adjust birth and death rates to see how they change the shape of a country's population pyramid over time.

lessons.title: Migration
lessons.content:
Migration is the movement of people from one place to another to live or work. It can be 'Internal Migration' (moving within a country, such as from rural areas to cities) or 'External Migration' (moving between countries). People migrate for many reasons, often categorised as 'push factors' (things that make you want to leave, like lack of jobs or natural disasters) and 'pull factors' (things that attract you to a new place, like better pay or safety).

In the Caribbean, migration has a major impact on society. 'Brain Drain' occurs when highly skilled people (like doctors and teachers) migrate to wealthier countries, leaving a shortage of expertise at home. On the other hand, 'Remittances' (money sent back by migrants to their families) provide a vital source of income for many Caribbean households and contribute to the national economy.

CSEC Social Studies explores the causes and consequences of migration and its impact on the development of the region. You will discuss the experiences of Caribbean migrants abroad and the challenges and opportunities created by the movement of people across borders.
objectives: Identify types of migration
Analyse the push and pull factors

experiment.description: Push-Pull Magnet: Drag various factors (e.g., 'better jobs', 'natural disasters') to either the 'Push' or 'Pull' category for a virtual migrant.

lessons.title: Forms of Communication
lessons.content:
Communication is the process of exchanging information, ideas, and feelings. It can be 'Verbal' (using words, either spoken or written) or 'Non-verbal' (using body language, facial expressions, or symbols). In the modern world, 'Mass Media' (like television, radio, and newspapers) and digital technologies have transformed how we communicate.

The rise of the internet and social media has made communication faster and more accessible than ever before. However, it has also created a 'Digital Divide' — the gap between those who have access to modern technology and those who do not. This divide can impact education, job opportunities, and participation in the democratic process.

CSEC students will analyse the impact of different forms of communication on society and discuss the ethical issues related to media and technology. Understanding communication is essential for effective social interaction and for navigating the complex information landscape of the 21st century.
objectives: Distinguish between different forms of communication
Understand the impact of technology

experiment.description: Message Relay: Send a message through various mediums (letter, phone, internet) and compare the speed, cost, and reach.

lessons.title: Consumer Rights and Responsibilities
lessons.content:
A consumer is anyone who buys or uses goods and services. To protect people in the marketplace, most countries have laws defining 'Consumer Rights,' such as the right to safety, the right to be informed, and the right to redress (compensation if a product is faulty).

Along with these rights come 'Consumer Responsibilities.' This includes being a 'Smart Shopper' by comparing prices, reading product labels, and understanding contracts like 'Hire Purchase.' Consumers should also practise responsible 'Budgeting' to manage their money effectively and avoid excessive debt. Consumer protection agencies help enforce these rights and educate the public.

CSEC Social Studies students will learn about the rights and responsibilities of consumers and the role of agencies like the Bureau of Standards. You will also discuss the importance of ethical consumption and the impact of consumer choices on the environment and society.
objectives: Identify consumer rights
Understand the role of consumer protection agencies

experiment.description: Smart Shopper Challenge: Evaluate different product labels and contracts to identify misleading information and exercise consumer rights.

lessons.title: Caribbean Cultural Diversity
lessons.content:
Caribbean Cultural Diversity describes a region settled by people from several continents, whose culture is learned, shared and passed on rather than carried in the blood. Culture is the whole way of life of a people - its language, religion, food, music, dress, festivals, values and family patterns. Ethnicity is the group a person belongs to by ancestry and shared tradition, and the Caribbean's ethnicity includes the indigenous Taino and Kalinago peoples, Africans brought by the slave trade, Europeans, Indians brought as indentured labourers after emancipation, Chinese, Portuguese and people of Middle Eastern descent.

Creolisation is the process by which these traditions mixed to make something new that belongs to the region: the creole languages usually called patois, pan music from steel, calypso and soca out of carnival, and a kitchen that put curry, saltfish, rice and peas and ackee on the same table. Cultural Retention is the other half of the story: traditions that survived almost intact, such as Kumina and Jonkonnu in Jamaica, Hosay in Trinidad, the nine-night ceremony, and the church and school festivals that mark Christmas and Easter.

Cultural Heritage is what a society chooses to keep and pass on, and it is held in two places: in monuments, museums, archives, songs and recipes, which is tangible and intangible heritage, and in people, through language, craft and ceremony. Caribana and Carnival, the Jamaica Folk Singers, the National Dance Theatre Company and the national libraries all exist to keep it alive.

Diversity is not a list to memorise but a reason for tolerance: the region's religions include Christianity, Hinduism, Islam, Judaism and Rastafari, and its languages include English, French, Dutch, Spanish and the creoles built from them. Culture also changes: globalisation, foreign media and migration push young people toward one world culture, while festivals, food and language pull them back, and a healthy society makes room for both.
objectives: Define culture and its elements
Explain the ethnic roots of Caribbean society
Describe Creolisation and Cultural Retention
Discuss how culture changes and why diversity needs tolerance

experiment.description: Where Did It Come From? Match each Caribbean tradition to its root.
